The history of computing is usually told as a sequence of machines, but it is just as much a history of abstractions. Early mechanical calculators could add and subtract, yet they had no notion of a program. Charles Babbage designed an engine that could be instructed by punched cards, and Ada Lovelace recognised that such a machine might manipulate symbols as well as numbers. A century later, electronic computers were wired by hand for each new problem until the stored-program idea made software a thing that could be written, copied and improved. Assemblers replaced raw machine code, and then compilers replaced assemblers for most work, translating expressive languages into instructions that a processor could execute directly. Each layer hid detail from the layer above it, and each layer made the whole stack easier to reason about while sometimes making it slower than a carefully tuned program written by an expert. Modern compilers recover much of that lost speed by building intermediate representations that expose structure: loops, memory accesses, data types and the dependencies between operations. Machine learning has added a new set of requirements to this picture. A neural network is a large graph of tensor operations, and the way those tensors are stored matters as much as the arithmetic performed on them. Quantised models store weights in only a few bits, which cuts memory traffic but demands kernels that can unpack and multiply them efficiently. In the most extreme case, each weight is just minus one, zero or one, and a matrix multiplication turns into additions and subtractions. Writing such kernels by hand for every processor is tedious, which is exactly why compiler infrastructure for low-bit models has become an active area of research.
